questions.q: The Earth completes one rotation on its own axis in about:
o: 24 hours
12 hours
7 days
30 days
questions.a: 24 hours. The Earth spins once on its own axis in about 24 hours; 12 hours is only about the length of daytime at many places, not of a full rotation.

questions.q: Seen from above the North Pole, in which way does the Earth rotate?
o: Anti-clockwise, that is, from West to East
Clockwise, that is, from West to East
Anti-clockwise, that is, from East to West
Clockwise, that is, from East to West
questions.a: Anti-clockwise, that is, from West to East. Viewed from the top of the North Pole, the Earth turns anti-clockwise, which is the West-to-East direction.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In India, sunrise occurs first in the eastern part of the country and then in the other parts.
Reason (R): The Earth rotates on its own axis from West to East.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: as the Earth turns from West to East, the eastern part of India is carried into the sunlit half first, so sunrise reaches it before the other parts.

questions.q: What is rotation? Name the imaginary line about which the Earth rotates, and the two points on the Earth through which it passes.
s: Rotation: the motion of an object in which all its parts move in circles around an imaginary line that passes through it
The Earth's axis of rotation, which passes through the geographic North Pole and South Pole
questions.a: Rotation is the motion of an object in which all its parts move in circles around an imaginary line passing through it. For the Earth this line is its axis of rotation, which passes through the geographic North Pole and the South Pole.

questions.q: True or False: At any moment, about half of the Earth's surface is having daytime. Give the verdict and a reason.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: sunlight falls only on the half of the Earth facing the Sun; that half has day and the other half has night
questions.a: True. Just as a torch lights only half of a globe, sunlight falls on the half of the Earth facing the Sun, which has daytime, while the other half is dark and has night.

questions.q: In a dark room, Farida shines a torch on a globe from about 1.5 m away and slowly turns the globe from West to East. A small sticker marks her town on the globe. (a) How much of the globe receives light at any moment? (b) What time of day does the lit part of the globe stand for? (c) What event in her town is shown when the sticker moves from the dark part into the light?
s: (a) About half of the globe is lit
(b) The lit half stands for daytime (the dark half for night)
(c) Sunrise in her town
questions.a: (a) About half of the globe receives light; the other half stays dark. (b) The lit half stands for daytime. (c) When the sticker moves from darkness into light, it shows sunrise in her town.

questions.q: Rotation is the motion in which all parts of an object move in circles around an imaginary line passing through the object itself. Which of these is an example of rotation?
o: A ceiling fan turning on its rod
The Earth moving around the Sun
The Moon moving around the Earth
A train moving along a straight track
questions.a: A ceiling fan turning on its rod: all its parts move in circles around a line through the fan itself, like a spinning top. The Earth going around the Sun and the Moon going around the Earth are revolutions, motions around another object.

questions.q: Rashmika sees that the shadows of coconut trees are long in the morning and shorter in the afternoon. She says, 'The shadows change because the Sun's position in the sky changes during the day, so the Sun must be travelling across the sky around the Earth.' Is she right, partly right or wrong? Explain.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: the Sun's position in the sky does change during the day, and this changes the shadows
Wrong part: the Sun only appears to move; the Earth's rotation from West to East makes it seem to cross the sky, as objects seem to turn round a merry-go-round rider
questions.a: Partly right. The Sun's position in the sky does change through the day, which changes the shadows. But the Sun only appears to travel across the sky: we watch it from the Earth, which is rotating from West to East, just as trees seem to turn around a person on a moving merry-go-round.

questions.q: In Kanniyakumari, Class VII measures the shadow of a 2-metre pole on one school day (invented data): 8 am, 3.4 m long and pointing West; 10 am, 1.2 m; 12 noon, 0.2 m; 2 pm, 1.1 m; 4 pm, 3.0 m long and pointing East. Their teacher reminds them that a shadow falls on the side away from the Sun. (a) At which reading was the Sun most nearly overhead? (b) In which direction was the Sun in the sky at 8 am? (c) Name the motion of the Earth that makes the Sun's position change during the day, and give its direction. (d) Nobody measured the shadow at 3 pm. Using the trend in the table, decide whether it was shorter or longer than 1.1 m and in which direction it pointed, with the reason.
s: (a) 12 noon, when the shadow was shortest
(b) In the East, since the shadow pointed West, away from the Sun
(c) Rotation of the Earth, from West to East
(d) Longer than 1.1 m (between 1.1 m and 3.0 m) and pointing East: after noon the shadow grows longer as the Sun appears to move towards the West
questions.a: (a) At 12 noon, when the shadow was shortest (0.2 m). (b) The Sun was in the East at 8 am, because the shadow pointed West, away from it. (c) The rotation of the Earth from West to East. (d) Longer than 1.1 m, somewhere between the 2 pm length (1.1 m) and the 4 pm length (3.0 m), and pointing East. After noon the shadows grow longer and point East, because the Sun appears to move towards the West as the afternoon goes on.

questions.q: Imagine that the Earth stopped rotating for a few days while the Sun stayed where it is (ignore the Earth's revolution, which changes little in a few days). Explain in four steps: (a) what a town on the half facing the Sun would have, day or night, and for how long; (b) whether people there would see the Sun move from East to West across the sky; (c) whether Rashmika's coconut-tree shadows in a sunlit place would change in length through the day; (d) whether eastern India would still see sunrise before western India each morning, with the reason.
s: (a) Daytime all the time, with no sunset, for as long as the Earth does not rotate
(b) No: the Sun would seem to stay at the same place in the sky, because its apparent motion comes from the Earth's rotation
(c) No: with the Sun's position fixed in the sky, the shadows would keep the same length and direction
(d) No: there would be no sunrise at all; sunrise happens only when rotation carries a place from the dark half into the lit half
questions.a: (a) It would have daytime all the time, with no sunset, because only the half facing the Sun is lit and nothing would carry the town into the dark half. (b) No. The Sun appears to move from East to West only because the Earth rotates from West to East; without rotation it would seem to stay in one place. (c) No. The Sun's position in the sky would not change, so the shadows would keep the same length and direction all day. (d) No. There would be no sunrise anywhere: sunrise happens as a place is carried from the dark half into the lit half by the rotation, so without rotation the question of which part sees it first does not arise.

questions.q: In Activity 12.3, students sketch the position of a group of stars called the Big Dipper. What is its Indian name?
o: Saptarishi
Dhruva Tara
Surya Siddhanta
Aryabhatiya
questions.a: Saptarishi. The Big Dipper is called Saptarishi; Dhruva Tara is the Pole Star, while Surya Siddhanta and Aryabhatiya are ancient texts on astronomy.

questions.q: Why does the Pole Star appear nearly stationary in the night sky?
o: The Earth's axis of rotation points very close to it
It is the star closest to the Earth
It goes round the Earth once in every 24 hours
It is the brightest star in the night sky
questions.a: The Earth's axis of rotation points very close to the Pole Star, so as the Earth rotates the Pole Star seems to stay nearly in one place while the other stars appear to move around it.

questions.q: (a) Name the ancient Indian astronomer who explained the apparent daily motion of the stars, and the treatise in which he did so. (b) What value did he give for the time the Earth takes to complete one rotation?
s: (a) Aryabhata, in the Aryabhatiya (around the fifth century CE)
(b) About 23 hours 56 minutes 4.1 seconds
questions.a: (a) Aryabhata explained it in his treatise Aryabhatiya, written around the fifth century CE. (b) He gave about 23 hours 56 minutes 4.1 seconds (in modern units) for one rotation, very close to the currently accepted value.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Aryabhata's value for the time the Earth takes to complete one rotation is slightly less than 24 hours.
Reason (R): Aryabhata explained the apparent motion of the stars due to the Earth's rotation in Verse 9 of the Golapada of the Aryabhatiya.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. Aryabhata's value, about 23 hours 56 minutes 4.1 seconds, is slightly less than 24 hours; R only says where he explained the apparent motion of the stars, which does not explain the size of his value.

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement I: Aryabhata compared the apparent motion of the stars to a man in a moving boat who sees stationary objects moving backwards.
Statement II: In the Northern Hemisphere, the Earth's axis of rotation points very close to the Big Dipper (Saptarishi), so the Big Dipper appears nearly stationary.
Statement III: In the middle of the nineteenth century, Leon Foucault used a long pendulum to give the first simple demonstration of the Earth's rotation.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: I and III only
I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III
questions.a: Statements I and III are correct. Statement II is wrong: the axis points very close to the Pole Star (Dhruva Tara), which appears nearly stationary, while the Big Dipper appears to move around it.

questions.q: Kavya points her camera at the northern sky from Mahuli in Maharashtra and keeps the shutter open for a long time. In the photograph each star shows up as a curved streak. (a) What are these streaks called, and what shape are they? (b) What do the streaks record, and what causes it? (c) Her friend photographs the same sky with the shutter open for only a fraction of a second. Will the stars show up as streaks? Explain.
s: (a) Star trails; they are arcs of circles
(b) They record the apparent motion of the stars, which is caused by the Earth's rotation
(c) No, the stars will show up as points: in a fraction of a second they hardly appear to move, so no trail is recorded
questions.a: (a) They are star trails, which are arcs of circles. (b) They record the apparent motion of the stars across the sky while the shutter is open; this apparent motion is caused by the Earth's rotation. (c) No. With the shutter open for only a fraction of a second, the stars hardly appear to move, so each star is recorded as a point and not as a trail; a trail needs a long exposure.

questions.q: Aisha in Pune plans to do Activity 12.3. Answer each part in one line. (a) Between which months does the activity ask her to look for the Big Dipper in the early evening? (b) Name the star around which the Big Dipper appears to move, with its Indian name. (c) How long should she wait between two sketches, and must all the sketches be made on the same night? (d) What will her sketches show the Big Dipper doing? (e) Which motion of the Earth causes what she sees?
s: (a) Between March and May
(b) The Pole Star, Dhruva Tara
(c) Two hours; yes, all on the same night
(d) The Big Dipper appears to move around the Pole Star
(e) The rotation of the Earth
questions.a: (a) On an early evening between March and May. (b) The Pole Star, called Dhruva Tara. (c) She should sketch every two hours, and all the sketches must be made on the same night. (d) The sketches will show the Big Dipper appearing to move around the Pole Star. (e) This apparent motion is caused by the Earth's rotation.

questions.q: Ishaan in Pune does Activity 12.3 on one April night. His notes on the Big Dipper are (invented data): 8 pm, low in the Northeast; 10 pm, higher in the Northeast; 12 midnight, high in the North, above the Pole Star; 2 am, in the Northwest; 4 am, low in the Northwest. Through the night the Pole Star stays in the same place. (a) Around which star does the Big Dipper appear to turn? (b) From which side of the northern sky to which side did the Big Dipper move between 8 pm and 4 am? (c) Compare this with the Sun's apparent motion in the day, and name the one cause of both. (d) His cousin sketches the Big Dipper only at 8 pm on two nights in a row. Will her two sketches look very different? Give the reason.
s: (a) The Pole Star (Dhruva Tara)
(b) From the eastern side (Northeast) to the western side (Northwest)
(c) Like the Sun, it appears to move from the East side towards the West; both are caused by the Earth's rotation from West to East
(d) No, nearly the same: in about 24 hours the Earth completes one rotation, so the sky is back at almost the same position
questions.a: (a) The Pole Star, called Dhruva Tara. (b) It moved from the Northeast, on the eastern side, to the Northwest, on the western side. (c) The Sun also appears to move from the East to the West. Both apparent motions are caused by the Earth rotating from West to East. (d) No. The two sketches are about 24 hours apart, which is about one full rotation of the Earth, so the Big Dipper is back at almost the same place.

questions.q: The Earth completes one revolution around the Sun in about:
o: 365 days and 6 hours
24 hours
6 months
100 days
questions.a: 365 days and 6 hours. That is the time for one revolution around the Sun; about 24 hours is the time for one rotation on the Earth's own axis.

questions.q: True or False: If you look at the same part of the night sky at 9 pm on 1 March and again at 9 pm on 1 April, you will see the star patterns in exactly the same places. Give the verdict and a reason.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: as the Earth revolves around the Sun, we look out in different directions through the year, so the stars seen at a fixed time of night gradually change from month to month
questions.a: False. The Earth keeps revolving around the Sun, so over the month we look out in a slightly different direction at 9 pm. The stars seen at a fixed time of night therefore change gradually, and the patterns will not be in exactly the same places a month later.

questions.q: (a) Name the motion of the Earth around the Sun, and the word for the path it follows. (b) Name one natural object that revolves around the Earth.
s: (a) Revolution; the path is called its orbit
(b) The Moon
questions.a: (a) The Earth's motion around the Sun is called revolution, and the path it takes is its orbit. (b) The Moon, the Earth's natural satellite, revolves around the Earth.

questions.q:
Match each term in Column A with its meaning in Column B.
Column A: 1. Rotation  2. Revolution  3. Orbit  4. Axis of rotation
Column B: (p) the motion of an object around another object  (q) the motion in which all parts of an object move in circles around an imaginary line through it  (r) the path an object takes while revolving around another object  (s) for the Earth, the imaginary line through the geographic North Pole and South Pole
questions.a: 1-q, 2-p, 3-r, 4-s: rotation is motion in circles around an imaginary line through the object; revolution is motion around another object; the orbit is the path of that revolution; the Earth's axis of rotation passes through its geographic North and South Poles.

questions.q: In a class model, Tara (the Earth) walks slowly in a big circle around a lamp (the Sun) while also turning round and round on the spot. Which statement about the model is correct?
o: Walking around the lamp shows revolution, which takes the Earth about 365 days and 6 hours
Turning on the spot shows revolution, which takes the Earth about 365 days and 6 hours
Walking around the lamp shows rotation, which takes the Earth about 24 hours
Turning on the spot shows rotation, which takes the Earth about 365 days and 6 hours
questions.a: Walking around the lamp shows revolution, the motion of one object around another, which takes the Earth about 365 days and 6 hours; turning on the spot shows rotation, which takes about 24 hours.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The stars that rise in the East at sunset in June are different from those that rise at sunset in December.
Reason (R): As the Earth revolves around the Sun, we look out in different directions after sunset at different times of the year.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: because the Earth moves along its orbit, the direction we face after sunset changes over the year, so different stars rise at sunset in different months.

questions.q: Lalit's calendar club notes that the Earth takes about 365 days and 6 hours to go once around the Sun. (a) Write this time in hours. (b) A wall calendar of exactly 365 days falls short of one revolution by how many hours? (c) After four revolutions, by how many hours, and so by how many whole days, has such a calendar fallen behind?
s: (b) 6 hours short each revolution
(c) 4 x 6 = 24 hours, which is 1 whole day
questions.a: (a) 365 x 24 = 8,760 hours, plus 6 hours, gives 8,766 hours. (b) A 365-day calendar is 6 hours short of one revolution. (c) Over four revolutions it falls behind by 4 x 6 = 24 hours, which is one whole day.

questions.q: Ira holds a round bangle a little below eye level and looks at it from the side; then she looks at it from straight above. (a) What shape does the bangle seem to have from each view? (b) A Solar System poster, drawn as seen from the side, shows the Earth's path around the Sun as a long, flat oval. What is the real shape of the Earth's orbit when seen from the top? (c) A diagram that explains the seasons is also drawn from the side, even though the orbit then looks stretched. What does a side view show clearly that a view from straight above would not?
s: (a) From the side it looks like a flat oval; from straight above it looks round
(b) Nearly circular: the orbit only looks elongated because the poster is a side view
(c) The tilt of the Earth's axis with respect to the orbit, that is, which hemisphere leans towards the Sun and which away from it
questions.a: (a) From the side the round bangle looks like a flat oval; from straight above it looks round. (b) Seen from the top, the Earth's orbit is nearly circular; the poster makes it look elongated only because it is a side view. (c) A side view shows the tilt of the Earth's axis with respect to the orbit, so one can see which hemisphere leans towards the Sun (the Northern in June) and which leans away; the seasons depend on this tilt.

questions.q: Megha lives in a village in the Tapi Valley. Her grandmother says that when a certain star pattern is seen rising in the East just after sunset, it is time to get ready for the monsoon. Megha watches the eastern sky and writes (invented data): 1 April, the pattern is not up at sunset and rises only late at night; 1 May, it rises at about 9 pm; 1 June, it is rising just as the sky gets dark after sunset. (a) Which motion of the Earth makes the pattern rise and climb the sky during one night? (b) Which motion of the Earth makes it rise at a different time each month? (c) About when will the pattern again be rising just after sunset? Give the reason. (d) On 1 July, will the pattern be below the eastern horizon, just rising, or already up in the sky at sunset? Use the trend in her notes.
s: (a) Rotation of the Earth
(b) Revolution of the Earth around the Sun
(c) Around 1 June next year, after one revolution of about 365 days and 6 hours
(d) Already up in the sky: each month it rises earlier, so by 1 July it has risen before sunset
questions.a: (a) The Earth's rotation makes it rise in the East and climb the sky during a night. (b) The Earth's revolution makes the stars seen after sunset change from month to month. (c) Around 1 June of the next year, after one full revolution of about 365 days and 6 hours. (d) Already up in the sky. Her notes show it rising earlier each month (late night, then 9 pm, then at dusk), so by 1 July it will have risen before sunset and will be above the eastern horizon when the sky gets dark.

questions.q: Seasons occur on the Earth because of:
o: the tilt of the Earth's axis and the Earth's spherical shape
the Earth coming much closer to the Sun in summer
the rotation of the Earth once in about 24 hours
the Moon blocking some of the sunlight in winter
questions.a: The tilt of the Earth's axis of rotation and the spherical shape of the Earth give rise to seasons; the small change in the Earth's distance from the Sun is not the reason.

questions.q: Which statement about the Southern Hemisphere in June is correct?
o: It has winter, because it is tilted away from the Sun
It has summer, because it is tilted towards the Sun
It has summer, because the Earth is closest to the Sun in June
It has winter, because the Earth is farthest from the Sun in June
questions.a: It has winter, because in June the Southern Hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun; the seasons there are the reverse of those in the Northern Hemisphere, and distance from the Sun is not the cause.

questions.q: (a) In which month is the Northern Hemisphere tilted towards the Sun? (b) Give the two reasons why that hemisphere is warmer in that month.
s: (a) June
(b) The same sunrays are spread over a smaller area, so the sunlight is more intense; and the daytime lasts more than 12 hours
questions.a: (a) June. (b) Because of the Earth's spherical shape, a given amount of sunrays falls on a smaller area there, so it is more intense; and that hemisphere receives sunlight for more than 12 hours a day. More intense sunlight for a longer time causes summer.

questions.q: True or False: The Earth's axis of rotation is tilted with respect to its orbit, and the Earth keeps this tilt as it goes around the Sun. Give the verdict and a reason.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the axis is not upright but tilted, and the tilt is kept all round the orbit; so the Northern Hemisphere leans towards the Sun in June and away from it in December
questions.a: True. The Earth's axis is not upright with respect to its orbit but tilted, and the Earth maintains this tilt as it orbits the Sun. Because the tilt is kept, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun in June and away from it in December.

questions.q: Jaya shines a torch straight down on a sheet of paper and sees a small, bright patch of light. When she tilts the torch, the same light spreads into a larger, dimmer patch. In June, which part of the Earth is like the larger, dimmer patch?
o: The Southern Hemisphere, which gets less intense sunlight
The Northern Hemisphere, which gets more intense sunlight
The North Pole, which is in darkness for all 24 hours
The equator, where seasons change the most
questions.a: The Southern Hemisphere: in June the same amount of sunrays is spread over a larger area there, so the sunlight is less intense, just like the larger, dimmer patch.

questions.q: Sameer says, 'In June the Earth is at its closest to the Sun, and that is why Delhi has summer in June.' Is he right, partly right or wrong? Explain using the chapter.
s: Verdict: wrong; the Earth is not closest to the Sun in June
The Earth is in fact closest to the Sun in January, when Delhi has winter, and the difference in distance is very small
The real reasons: in June the Northern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, so the sunlight falls on a smaller area (more intense) and lasts more than 12 hours
questions.a: Wrong. The Earth is not closest to the Sun in June: it is closest in January, when Delhi has winter, and the change in distance over the year is very small. Delhi has summer in June because the Northern Hemisphere is then tilted towards the Sun, so the same sunrays fall on a smaller area (more intense sunlight) for more than 12 hours a day.

questions.q: In June, Tanvi in Lucknow writes to her pen-pal Olivia in Cape Town, South Africa, a city in the Southern Hemisphere. Tanvi writes, 'It is very hot here and the Sun stays up for nearly 14 hours.' Olivia replies, 'It is cold here and we get only about 10 hours of sunlight.' (The hours are invented.) (a) Which hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun in June? (b) Name the season each girl is having. (c) Which season will each girl have in December? (d) Apart from the longer day, give one more reason why Lucknow is hotter than Cape Town in June.
s: (a) The Northern Hemisphere
(b) Tanvi: summer; Olivia: winter
(c) Tanvi: winter; Olivia: summer
(d) In Lucknow the same sunrays fall on a smaller area, so the sunlight is more intense
questions.a: (a) The Northern Hemisphere, where Lucknow is. (b) Tanvi is having summer and Olivia winter. (c) In December it is reversed: winter for Tanvi and summer for Olivia. (d) In June the same amount of sunrays is spread over a smaller area in the Northern Hemisphere, so the sunlight in Lucknow is more intense.

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement I: In December, places in the Northern Hemisphere are in darkness for more than 12 hours of the Earth's 24-hour rotation.
Statement II: In June, the Northern Hemisphere has summer because, being tilted towards the Sun, it is much closer to the Sun.
Statement III: The change in the Earth's distance from the Sun during a year is very small.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: I and III only
I only
II and III only
I, II and III
questions.a: Statements I and III are correct. Statement II is one of the incorrect reasons often given for seasons: the difference in distance is very small. The Northern Hemisphere has summer in June because the same sunrays fall on a smaller area there and the daytime lasts more than 12 hours.

questions.q: For a model of the seasons, Ravi carries a globe with a tilted axis around a lamp. At every position he turns the globe so that its North Pole leans towards the lamp. (a) What would his model wrongly show for the Northern Hemisphere through the whole year? (b) Which fact about the Earth's tilt has Ravi ignored? (c) How should he move the globe instead? (d) In the corrected model, at the position for December, which hemisphere gets the more intense light? (e) In that December position, how many hours of light does the North Pole get while the globe turns once?
s: (a) Summer in the Northern Hemisphere all year, with no change of seasons
(b) The Earth keeps the same tilt as it orbits the Sun
(c) Keep the axis tilted the same way in the room at every position
(d) The Southern Hemisphere
(e) No light at all: the North Pole is in darkness for all 24 hours
questions.a: (a) His model keeps the Northern Hemisphere tilted towards the lamp all the time, so it wrongly shows summer there all year, with no seasons. (b) The Earth maintains its tilt as it orbits the Sun; the axis does not swing round to face the Sun. (c) He should keep the axis tilted in the same direction in the room at every position around the lamp. (d) In the December position the Southern Hemisphere is tilted towards the lamp and gets the more intense light. (e) None: in December the North Pole stays in darkness for all 24 hours of a rotation.

questions.q: In the Northern Hemisphere, the longest day of the year falls around:
o: 21 June, the summer solstice
22 December, the winter solstice
21 March, the spring equinox
23 September, the autumn equinox
questions.a: 21 June, the summer solstice. After it the days become shorter; the shortest day is around 22 December, and on the equinoxes the daytime is 12 hours.

questions.q:
Match each place and time in Column A with what it experiences in Column B.
Column A: 1. A town on the equator, in any month  2. The North Pole, in June  3. The North Pole, in December  4. Bhopal, on 21 June
Column B: (p) about 12 hours of daylight, with little change through the year  (q) the Sun in the sky for all 24 hours  (r) darkness for all 24 hours  (s) the longest daytime of its year
questions.a: 1-p, 2-q, 3-r, 4-s: the equator always has 12 hours of sunlight and 12 of darkness; the North Pole gets sunlight for all 24 hours in June and is dark for all 24 hours in December; 21 June, the summer solstice, is Bhopal's longest day.

questions.q: (a) What is the day around 22 December called in the Northern Hemisphere, and what is special about it? (b) What happens to the lengths of the day and the night after 21 June?
s: (a) The winter solstice: the shortest day and longest night of the year
(b) The days become shorter and the nights longer
questions.a: (a) It is the winter solstice, when the Northern Hemisphere has its shortest day and longest night. (b) After the summer solstice on 21 June, the days become shorter and the nights become longer.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): For the southern states of India, the effect of seasons is not very prominent.
Reason (R): Places on the equator have 12 hours of daylight only on the two equinox days.
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: A is true, but R is false. On the equator there are always 12 hours of sunlight and 12 hours of darkness, in every month, with little change in intensity; that is why seasons are not very prominent in the southern states close to it.

questions.q: True or False: Like the North Pole, the South Pole has the Sun in its sky continuously from about 21 March to 22 September. Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the South Pole has the opposite; it is dark during those months and has continuous sunshine for the other six months (about 22 September to 21 March)
questions.a: False. The South Pole experiences the opposite of the North Pole: while the Sun stays up at the North Pole from about 21 March to 22 September, the South Pole is in darkness, and it gets its six months of continuous sunshine during the other half of the year.

questions.q: Neha in Bhopal finds that the daytime was about 13 hours on 1 May and again about 13 hours on 1 August (rounded). (a) Between these two dates, around which date was the daytime longest, and what is that day called? (b) On 1 August, were the days getting longer or shorter? (c) Will Bhopal's daytime on 1 November be more or less than 12 hours? Give the reason.
s: (a) Around 21 June, the summer solstice
(b) Shorter: after the summer solstice the days become shorter and the nights longer
(c) Less than 12 hours: 1 November comes after the autumn equinox (23 September), when daytime is 12 hours, and the days keep getting shorter until 22 December
questions.a: (a) Around 21 June, the summer solstice, which is the longest day in the Northern Hemisphere. (b) Shorter: after the summer solstice the duration of the day becomes shorter and the night longer. (c) Less than 12 hours. Daytime is 12 hours around the autumn equinox, 23 September, and it keeps getting shorter until the winter solstice around 22 December, so on 1 November it is under 12 hours.

questions.q: The daytime at four places on two dates is (invented data): Place V: 21 June, 13 h 10 min; 22 December, 10 h 50 min. Place Y: 21 June, 14 h 20 min; 22 December, 9 h 40 min. Place Z: 21 June, 24 h; 22 December, 0 h. Place W: 21 June, 9 h 50 min; 22 December, 14 h 10 min. (a) Which place is at or very near the North Pole? Give the reason. (b) Is Y in the Northern or the Southern Hemisphere? Give the reason. (c) About how long will Y's daytime be on 23 September? (d) Of V and Y, which is nearer the equator? Decide using the data and what the chapter says about daytime on the equator. (e) In which month, June or December, does W have its summer? Give the reason.
s: (a) Z: sunlight for all 24 hours in June and darkness for all 24 hours in December
(b) Northern: its daytime is longer than 12 hours in June and shorter in December
(c) About 12 hours, since 23 September is the autumn equinox

(d) V: its daytime moves only 1 h 10 min away from 12 hours, while Y's moves 2 h 20 min; the equator always has 12 hours and the pole swings from 24 h to 0 h, so the smaller swing is nearer the equator
(e) December: W's daytime is longer than 12 hours in December, so it is in the Southern Hemisphere, where the seasons are reversed
questions.a: (a) Z, because it has sunlight for all 24 hours in June and darkness for all 24 hours in December, like the North Pole. (b) Northern Hemisphere: Y's daytime is longer than 12 hours in June and shorter in December. (c) About 12 hours, because 23 September is the autumn equinox. (d) V. On the equator the daytime is always 12 hours, while at the North Pole it swings all the way from 24 hours to 0 hours. V's daytime moves only 1 h 10 min away from 12 hours (13 h 10 min and 10 h 50 min), while Y's moves 2 h 20 min (14 h 20 min and 9 h 40 min), so V is nearer the equator. (e) December. W has more than 12 hours of daytime in December and less in June, so it is in the Southern Hemisphere, where the seasons and length of daytime are reversed: summer comes in December.

questions.q: A solar eclipse occurs when:
o: the Moon comes between the Sun and the Earth
the Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon
the Sun comes between the Earth and the Moon
Venus comes between the Sun and the Earth
questions.a: The Moon comes between the Sun and the Earth and stops the Sun's light from reaching us. When the Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon, it is a lunar eclipse.

questions.q: Which is the safest way for a student to watch a solar eclipse?
o: Join a planetarium's viewing event that gives special eye protection
Look at the Sun through a pair of very dark sunglasses
Look at the Sun through a pair of binoculars
Look straight at the Sun for only a few seconds
questions.a: Join an eclipse-viewing event of a planetarium or astronomy club, which provides specialised eye protection for solar viewing. Even during an eclipse the Sun can damage the eyes, so it must not be viewed directly or through sunglasses, binoculars or telescopes.

questions.q: What is meant by the apparent size of an object? On which two things does it depend?
s: Apparent size: the size of an object as seen by our eye
It depends on the object's actual physical size and its distance from us
questions.a: Apparent size is the size of an object as seen by the eye. It depends on both the actual physical size of the object and its distance from the observer.

questions.q: (a) What do observers see during a total solar eclipse? (b) What do observers see during a partial solar eclipse? (c) Why is a total solar eclipse seen at a place for only a few minutes?
s: (a) The Sun is completely hidden; their area is in total darkness, in the Moon's shadow
(b) The Moon blocks out only some parts of the Sun
(c) The Moon's shadow moves across the Earth's surface because of the Earth's rotation and the Moon's motion in its orbit
questions.a: (a) In a total solar eclipse the observers are in the Moon's shadow; no part of the Sun can be seen and it turns dark during the day. (b) In a partial solar eclipse the Moon blocks out only some regions of the Sun. (c) Because of the Earth's rotation and the Moon's motion in its orbit, the Moon's shadow moves across the Earth, so totality at one place lasts only a few minutes.

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement I: A Transit of Venus, when Venus passes between the Sun and the Earth, is a rare event.
Statement II: Not eating or not going out during a solar eclipse has a scientific basis.
Statement III: The Surya Siddhanta is an ancient Indian text that provides calculations to predict eclipses.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: I and III only
I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III
questions.a: Statements I and III are correct. Statement II is wrong: such practices are superstitions from the time when the cause of eclipses was not known; now that we know why a solar eclipse occurs, we need not fear it, as long as we do not look at the Sun directly.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Mercury and Venus can block the entire light of the Sun because they are larger than the Moon.
Reason (R): Mercury and Venus are much farther from the Earth than the Moon is.
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
questions.a: A is false, but R is true. Mercury and Venus are larger than the Moon, but because they are much farther away their apparent sizes are very small, so they never block the whole Sun; Venus appears only as a tiny black dot during a Transit of Venus.

questions.q: Leena stands at a place where a total solar eclipse will be seen. As the eclipse begins, the Moon slowly moves across the Sun. In which order will she see the events?
o: Partial eclipse, total eclipse, 'diamond ring', partial eclipse, full daylight
Total eclipse, partial eclipse, 'diamond ring', full daylight
'Diamond ring', total eclipse, partial eclipse, full daylight
Partial eclipse, 'diamond ring', partial eclipse, total eclipse
questions.a: Partial eclipse, total eclipse, 'diamond ring', partial eclipse, full daylight. The Moon first covers part of the Sun, then all of it; the 'diamond ring' is seen just as the Moon starts to move away after totality; then a partial eclipse is seen again as daylight returns.

questions.q: Dr Meera, an astronomer in Bengaluru, plans to fly to another country to watch a total solar eclipse that cannot be seen from India. (a) Why can a total solar eclipse not be seen from every place on the Earth's day side, so that she has to travel? (b) Why do scientists take such trouble to observe eclipses?
s: (a) The Moon's shadow falls only on a small area of the Earth's surface, and only there is the Sun completely hidden
(b) Eclipses give scientists an opportunity to study phenomena that cannot be observed otherwise
questions.a: (a) During a solar eclipse the Moon's shadow falls on only a small area of the Earth's surface; only observers in that area see a total solar eclipse, so she must travel there. (b) Scientists go around the world to observe eclipses because eclipses give them an opportunity to study phenomena that cannot be observed otherwise.

questions.q: Standing at the back of the school hall, Imran closes one eye and holds a one-rupee coin at arm's length towards the round clock on the front wall. The coin just hides the whole clock face, although the clock face is many times wider than the coin. He uses this as a model of a solar eclipse. (a) Which object stands for the Sun and which for the Moon? (b) Why can the small coin hide the much larger clock face? (c) Imran walks up until he is about 2 m from the clock and again holds the coin at arm's length. Can it still hide the whole clock face? Explain. (d) His younger sister, whose arm is shorter, stands where Imran first stood and holds an identical coin at her arm's length. Will her coin hide the clock face completely or only part of it? Explain.
s: (a) The clock face stands for the Sun and the coin for the Moon
(b) Apparent size depends on both actual size and distance; the coin is much closer to the eye, so its apparent size matches that of the far clock face
(c) No: the clock is now much nearer, so its apparent size becomes far larger than the coin's and the coin hides only part of it
(d) Completely: her coin is nearer to her eye than Imran's was, so it looks larger than in Imran's first try, where it just hid the clock face
questions.a: (a) The clock face stands for the Sun and the coin for the Moon. (b) The apparent size of an object depends on both its actual size and its distance from the eye. The coin is much closer, so it looks about as large as the distant clock face, just as the small but near Moon looks as large as the huge but far Sun. (c) No. At about 2 m the clock face is much nearer, so its apparent size becomes far larger than the coin's, and the coin can hide only part of it. (d) Completely. Her shorter arm keeps the coin nearer to her eye than Imran's coin was, so it looks larger than in his first try, where it only just hid the clock face; it now more than covers the face.

questions.q: For a solar eclipse, Ms Fernandes sets up a projector on the school ground in Ooty: a hollow ball half-filled with sand, with a small embroidery mirror stuck on it, resting on an adhesive-tape ring. The mirror throws the Sun's image onto a white screen about 4 m away, and around 40 students watch the screen together. (a) Why is the ball half-filled with sand? (b) During the eclipse the Sun's image slowly drifts off the screen. Why? (c) How does the tape ring help with the problem in (b)? (d) Lata wants to check the alignment by looking into the mirror; Om wants to turn the ball while watching only the screen. Whose way should the teacher allow, and why?
s: (a) The sand keeps the ball stable
(b) The Earth keeps rotating, so the Sun's position in the sky keeps changing and the reflected image moves
(c) On the ring the ball can be turned easily to bring the image back, since holding a mirror at the right angle throughout the eclipse is difficult
(d) Om's: looking into the mirror would send the reflected sunlight into Lata's eyes, which the chapter warns against
questions.a: (a) The sand keeps the ball stable. (b) As the Earth rotates, the Sun's position in the sky keeps changing, so the reflected image slowly moves off the screen. (c) On the tape ring the ball can be turned around easily to bring the image back; holding a mirror at the correct angle throughout an eclipse is difficult. (d) Om's way. Looking into the mirror would send the reflected sunlight straight into Lata's eyes; the chapter warns never to direct the reflected beam into anyone's eyes, and the activity must be run under the teacher's supervision.

questions.q: During a total lunar eclipse, the Moon appears:
o: dark red
completely invisible
brighter than usual
pale blue
questions.a: Dark red. When the Moon is completely in the Earth's shadow, its bright disc turns dark red and stays so until it moves out of the shadow.

questions.q: During a lunar eclipse, the Sun, the Earth and the Moon lie in a line in which order?
o: Sun, Earth, Moon
Sun, Moon, Earth
Earth, Sun, Moon
Moon, Sun, Earth
questions.a: Sun, Earth, Moon: the Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon and blocks sunlight from reaching the Moon. Sun, Moon, Earth is the order in a solar eclipse.

questions.q: (a) Who is known as the father of modern Indian astronomy? (b) Name two places in India where telescopes were set up through his efforts.
s: (a) M.K. Vainu Bappu
(b) Manora Peak near Nainital (Uttarakhand) and Kavalur (Tamil Nadu)
questions.a: (a) M.K. Vainu Bappu. (b) He led the setting up of telescopes at Manora Peak near Nainital in Uttarakhand and at Kavalur in Tamil Nadu; the Kavalur observatory is named after him.

questions.q: Compare a total solar eclipse with a total lunar eclipse under four headings: (i) which body comes in between the other two; (ii) whose shadow falls on which body; (iii) whether it is safe to watch with the naked eye; (iv) whether the total eclipse is seen from a small area or a large part of the Earth.
s: (i) Solar: the Moon comes between the Sun and the Earth; lunar: the Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon
(ii) Solar: the Moon's shadow falls on the Earth; lunar: the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon
(iii) Solar: never safe with the naked eye; lunar: safe with the naked eye
(iv) Total solar: a small area of the Earth; total lunar: a large part of the Earth
questions.a: (i) In a solar eclipse the Moon is between the Sun and the Earth; in a lunar eclipse the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon. (ii) In a solar eclipse the Moon's shadow falls on a small area of the Earth; in a lunar eclipse the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. (iii) A solar eclipse must never be viewed directly, but an eclipsed full Moon can be watched safely with the naked eye. (iv) A total solar eclipse is seen only from a small part of the Earth, while a lunar eclipse can be seen from a large part of it.

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement I: When part of the Moon is in the Earth's shadow and the rest of it is visible, it is called a partial lunar eclipse.
Statement II: M.K. Vainu Bappu mainly studied the Moon.
Statement III: The Kodaikanal Solar Observatory is operated by the Indian Institute of Astrophysics, Bengaluru.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: I and III only
I only
II and III only
I, II and III
questions.a: Statements I and III are correct. Statement II is wrong: Vainu Bappu mainly studied stars and even discovered a comet.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A lunar eclipse can be seen from a large part of the Earth.
Reason (R): During a total lunar eclipse, the Moon appears dark red.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. The colour of the eclipsed Moon does not explain why so many people can see it; that comes from the Earth's shadow falling on the Moon, which anyone who can see the Moon at that time can watch.

questions.q: Sneha wants to watch the next lunar eclipse from her terrace in Guwahati. (a) Name a free app she can use on a computer to find out about eclipses visible from her location. (b) During the eclipse the whole bright disc of the Moon turns dark red. What is this kind of lunar eclipse called, and until when does the Moon stay dark red?
s: (a) The computer version of the Stellarium app
(b) A total lunar eclipse; the Moon stays dark red until it moves out of the Earth's shadow
questions.a: (a) The free computer version of the Stellarium app gives information about upcoming solar and lunar eclipses visible from her location. (b) It is a total lunar eclipse, when the Moon is completely in the Earth's shadow; the Moon stays dark red until it moves out of the Earth's shadow.

questions.q: The astronomy club of a school in Nagpur pins up a notice about next year's eclipses (invented). Event 1: 'March: the Moon will pass completely into the Earth's shadow and turn dark red.' Event 2: 'May: a lunar eclipse on a half-Moon night.' Event 3: 'August: a solar eclipse. Our town lies outside the small area on which the Moon's shadow falls, but the Moon will hide a part of the Sun from here. Members may watch it through dark sunglasses or binoculars.' Evaluate the notice: (a) Name the kind of eclipse in Event 1 and the body that lies between the other two. (b) Decide whether Event 2 can be correct, with the reason. (c) Name the kind of eclipse the town will see in Event 3, and say why the town will not see the Sun completely hidden. (d) Is the viewing advice for Event 3 safe? Give the reason. (e) The club can borrow specialised eye protection from a planetarium for only one of the eclipses. For which event should it use the protection, and why is it not needed for the other?
s: (a) A total lunar eclipse; the Earth lies between the Sun and the Moon
(b) Not correct: a lunar eclipse is seen on a full Moon night, when the Earth's shadow falls on the full disc of the Moon
(c) A partial solar eclipse: the Sun is completely hidden only in the small area on which the Moon's shadow falls
(d) Not safe: even during an eclipse the Sun is intense enough to damage the eyes and cause blindness; it must not be viewed through sunglasses or binoculars
(e) Event 3, the solar eclipse; the eclipsed full Moon of Event 1 can be watched safely with the naked eye
questions.a: (a) Event 1 is a total lunar eclipse, with the Earth between the Sun and the Moon, so the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. (b) Event 2 cannot be correct: in a lunar eclipse we see the Earth's shadow falling on the full disc of the Moon, so it happens on a full Moon night, not a half-Moon night. (c) The town will see a partial solar eclipse. Only the small area on which the Moon's shadow falls sees the Sun completely hidden; elsewhere the Moon blocks only some regions of the Sun. (d) No. Even during an eclipse the Sun is intense enough to damage the eyes and cause blindness, and the chapter says not to view it through sunglasses, binoculars or telescopes. (e) The protection should be used for Event 3, the solar eclipse. Unlike the Sun, the eclipsed full Moon in Event 1 can be watched safely with the naked eye.

questions.q: Rohan in Indore keeps a log of a lunar eclipse (invented data): 8:30 pm, the full Moon is bright; 9:20 pm, a dark curved shadow has just started to cover one edge; 10:30 pm, the whole Moon is dark red; 11:15 pm, the whole Moon is still dark red; 11:55 pm, one edge is bright again and the rest is dark; 1:05 am, the whole Moon is bright again. (a) What is the stage seen at 9:20 pm called? (b) Between which two log entries did the total eclipse begin? (c) From the log, what is the shortest time the total eclipse could have lasted, and what is the longest? (d) His friend says, 'A total eclipse lasts only a few minutes, so Rohan must have misread his watch.' Use the log and the chapter to decide whether the friend is right.
s: (a) A partial lunar eclipse: only part of the Moon is in the Earth's shadow
(b) Between 9:20 pm and 10:30 pm
(c) Shortest: 45 minutes (it was total at both 10:30 pm and 11:15 pm); longest: just under 2 hours 35 minutes (it began after 9:20 pm and ended before 11:55 pm)

(d) Not right: only a total solar eclipse lasts a few minutes at a place, because the Moon's shadow moves across the Earth; in a total lunar eclipse the Moon stays dark red until it moves out of the Earth's shadow, and the log shows at least 45 minutes
questions.a: (a) A partial lunar eclipse: part of the Moon is in the Earth's shadow and the rest is visible. (b) Between the 9:20 pm entry, when only one edge was covered, and the 10:30 pm entry, when the whole Moon was dark red. (c) The Moon was wholly dark red at 10:30 pm and at 11:15 pm, so the total eclipse lasted at least 11:15 - 10:30 = 45 minutes. It began after 9:20 pm and ended before 11:55 pm, so it lasted less than 2 hours 35 minutes. (d) The friend is not right. 'A few minutes' is true of a total solar eclipse at one place, because the Moon's shadow moves across the Earth's surface. In a total lunar eclipse the Moon stays dark red until it moves out of the Earth's shadow, and Rohan's log shows it dark red for at least 45 minutes.
